sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Efficient reinforcement learning often uses data generated by policy that differs from the current learner. Asynchronous reinforcement learning (async RL) creates this difference by running generation and training concurrently: while response is being generated, the learner can move on to newer policy. Reusing responses and refreshing the sampler less frequently further separate the learner πθ from the behavior policy µ that generated the data (Espeholt et al., 2018, Hilton et al., 2022). difference can also arise without any change in model weights. When training and inference use different numerical precision or execution kernels, they can assign different probabilities to the same action, creating mismatch between training and inference (TIM) (Yao et al., 2025). In both cases, training is off-policy: the data-generating distribution differs from the current learner. This matters because an update computed from behavior data may differ from the update the learner would obtain from its own responses. In agentic tasks, the difference can be larger when actions lead to different future states and rewards. Section 5.3 analyzes how task structure and policy staleness contribute to this effect. To account for this difference, importance sampling (IS) gives behavior samples more or less weight according to their probability under the learner. Full sequence-level IS uses the likelihood ratio of the complete response. When µ assigns positive probability to every response that πθ can generate, weighting behavior samples by this ratio gives an unbiased estimate of the learners reward gradient, but multiplying token ratios can produce extremely high variance (Owen, 2013). Practical sequencelevel methods such as GSPO stabilize the weights through length normalization and clipping (Zheng et al., 2025). Another way to avoid multiplying ratios across the response is to use token-level IS, which corrects only the distribution over the next action at history sampled under the behavior policy. Large token ratios can still cause high gradient variance (Bai et al., 2026b). To limit these extreme gradient contributions, truncated importance sampling (TIS) caps token weights at the cost of additional clipping bias (Ionides, 2008, MiniMax, 2025). Yet omitting or truncating the weights also leaves specific problem: parts of the reward that do not distinguish between actions can still drive the update. To see why, consider the learners score (gradient of its log-probability). Its mean is zero under the learners own action distribution, so reward baseline independent of the action makes no contribution to the gradient when sampling from the learner. By contrast, under the behavior policy, that mean need not be zero, allowing the same baseline to contribute to an update without full importance weighting. Score centering (SC) removes this contribution by subtracting the mean of the score under the behavior policy, or the mean of the weighted score under the behavior policy when combined with TIS (Marek and Ryabinin, 2026). This mean is taken over actions at the same history, and exact centering therefore cancels the unwanted contribution in expectation. In practice, Monte Carlo estimates approximate this conditional mean using auxiliary actions drawn at that history. However, removing the baseline contribution does not remove every difference between behavior data and learner responses, because the remaining token advantages still depend on continuations generated by µ. Even with single terminal reward, token can have different value when the learner completes the response differently. Although TIS limits the weight of the current token, it does not correct the distribution of the preceding history or the subsequent continuation. As the learner changes, improving the surrogate on behavior trajectories can therefore fail to improve the reward obtained from the learners own trajectories. This dependence on behavior continuations motivates limiting how far the learner moves from the behavior policy. We introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), family of methods that add reverse KL regularization to SC: RSC = SC + KL (+TIS). The family regularizes both SC 2 without IS and SC+TIS (Marek and Ryabinin, 2026). At each history, the KL penalty compares the learners next-token distribution with the behavior policys next-token distribution and encourages them to stay close. Because the behavior policy serves as the KL reference, refreshing it also updates the reference used by the penalty. RSC thus preserves SCs baseline correction while limiting movement away from the policy used to estimate token advantages. The same tokenlevel regularizer applies to both choices of reward weights and requires no additional environment interactions. To explain how regularization can help, our analysis connects accurate fitting of the regularized surrogate to improvement in expected reward. The two RSC variants use different proof arguments, but both turn accurate fitting into reward progress. Repeated fitting gives final policy whose reward from single response nearly matches the reward obtained by best-of-N sampling from the initial policy. Section 4.2 explains these results, with proofs and sample bounds in Appendix C. We then test whether this additional control helps when behavior data become less representative of the learner. Both agentic interaction and sampler staleness can amplify the consequences of policy mismatch. In agentic tasks, choosing different action can change later observations, the actions available afterward, and the eventual reward, so tokens advantage under behavior continuations may poorly represent its advantage under learner continuations. Staleness introduces the same difficulty by allowing more learner updates while the behavior policy remains fixed, changing both action probabilities and the continuations they induce. Section 5.3 examines these two effects through task structure and sampler refresh intervals. In these comparisons, RSC achieves substantially higher rewards than unregularized SC in agentic environments, while increasing the refresh interval weakens SC on Countdown and math tasks with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. On Countdown, these failures persist even with Monte Carlo centering. Beyond these controlled comparisons, we evaluate RSC on mathematical reasoning with dense and MoE models, and on agentic tasks spanning online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS attains substantially higher training rewards on Crafter and Craftax for the same number of sampled responses (Figure 7). In final evaluations, RSC with TIS achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks against baselines including IS-PPOClip, which combines importance sampling with PPO-style clipping. It raises AppWorlds mean evaluation the score of the strongest BabyAI baseline, score by 14.3% over SC and SC+TIS, and reaches 9.9 IS-PPOClip.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Score centering and off-policy learning. RL for language models creates mismatch between the learner and behavior policy through asynchronous generation, response reuse and different numerical implementations for training and inference (Fu et al., 2025, Yao et al., 2025). Engineering solutions align training and inference: kernels with batch invariance remove dependence on batch shape from normalization, matrix multiplication and attention (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), while consistent FP16 computation reduces rounding discrepancies (Qi et al., 2025). Alongside these engineering solutions, algorithmic methods correct updates computed from stale data. For example, IMPALA uses importance correction in asynchronous learning (Espeholt et al., 2018), and Hilton et al. (2022) separate the sampling policy from the proximal policy used to control updates. AReaL and AsyncWebRL adopt this separation, combining importance weights for data from earlier policies with PPO-style clipping around more recent policy (Schulman et al., 2017, Fu et al., 2025, Bai et al., 2026a). We include this combination as the IS-PPOClip baseline. TIS caps token importance weights (Ionides, 2008, Yao et al., 2025, MiniMax, 2025), IcePop masks token 3 corrections outside an interval (Ling Team et al., 2025), Sequence MIS (Liu et al., 2025) combines sequence-level importance weights with sequence-level mask, and GSPO clips length-normalized sequence ratio (Zheng et al., 2025). Adaptive Layerwise Perturbation (ALP) introduces learnable perturbations into each layers input hidden states and uses the perturbed learner in the numerator of the importance ratio to address policy staleness and mismatch between training and inference (Ye et al., 2026). SC adds different operation: subtracting the expectation of the learner score under the behavior policy, including the expectation of the weighted score when composed with TIS or MIS (Marek and Ryabinin, 2026). Exact centering removes the expected contribution of reward baseline independent of the action. RSC preserves this correction and penalizes movement away from the behavior policy. Policy optimization with KL regularization. Alongside corrections to the sampled update, KL regularization limits policy movement relative to reference distribution. Relative Entropy Policy Search and TRPO constrain distributional change (Peters et al., 2010, Schulman et al., 2015), with regularized MDP theory linking such updates to Bellman operators and mirror descent (Geist et al., 2019). In language model alignment, RLHF penalizes deviation from supervised reference (Stiennon et al., 2020, Ouyang et al., 2022), and DPO uses the closed-form optimizer of KL-regularized objective to learn from preference pairs (Rafailov et al., 2023). Theory for preference learning provides guarantees for finite samples in offline, online and hybrid settings (Xiong et al., 2024), including general preference oracles (Ye et al., 2024). Divergence choice and data coverage also shape learning: χ2 preference optimization addresses overoptimization of reward models (Huang et al., 2025), and the coverage principle relates pretraining coverage to posttraining success (Chen et al., 2026). Huang et al. (2026) study coverage collapse and establish convergence through KL regularization and resets of the reference policy, treating complete responses as actions and using sequence-level importance ratio. At the token level, Future-KL propagates subsequent tokens regularization costs into the update for the current token (Yao et al., 2026), while Proximal KL combines credit assignment for later tokens with token-level importance sampling and refreshed proximal reference policy (Bai et al., 2026b). RSC applies token-level reverse KL directly to the score centering objective, using the behavior policy as its reference. The same penalty applies to SC without IS and SC+TIS, preserving their correction for the reward baselines contribution.

sections.title: Identifying Failure Modes of Score Centering
sections.content: The reward guarantees in Section 4.2 rely on accurate fitting within specified policy neighborhood. In training, both the score center estimate and movement away from the behavior policy can affect learning. We examine these two potential sources of SC failure in turn. Section 5.2 shows that Monte Carlo centering improves learning over approximate centers. These improved estimates leave the dependence on behavior histories and continuations unchanged, motivating the task and staleness comparisons in Section 5.3. sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: In the controlled experiments in Figures 4 through 7, the sampler refresh interval controls how long the learner updates against fixed behavior policy. The learner πθ updates while µ remains fixed for updates. The sampler then copies the learner weights to refresh µ. In agentic experiments, rollout generation and learner training run concurrently: the learner consumes completed response groups from queue, taking one update per new batch while generation continues under fixed µ. Countdown alternates sampling and training within the same schedule with µ fixed. Larger therefore permits greater policy separation. sections.title: 5.2 Score Centering Fails Under Top-k Estimation
sections.content: Monte Carlo gives an unbiased estimate of the conditional center. The original SC implementation uses the 128 highest behavior probabilities and modeled tail (Marek and Ryabinin, 2026), introducing approximation bias. We replace this biased approximation with auxiliary draws from µ. At the history preceding each generated token, we draw auxiliary tokens independently with replacement from µ( h). These draws are independent of the generated action and the continuation of the response, and require no additional response generation or reward evaluation. Backpropagation through the average learner log-probability of the auxiliary tokens gives an unbiased estimate of Eµ[ψθ h]. For SC+TIS, each auxiliary log-probability receives its own detached ρTIS weight, giving an unbiased estimate of Eµ[ρTISψθ h]. If token is sampled more than once, each draw contributes to the estimate. Appendix lists the sample counts. Monte Carlo centering improves learning over top-k estimation. Every tested Monte Carlo variant in Figure 4 achieves higher final evaluation score than the corresponding Top128 baseline. The math comparisons show substantial evaluation gains with both BF16 and FP8 rollouts. At πθ = µ, the advantages and history distributions agree. When the relevant action and continuation distributions remain close, advantages under the behavior policy provide local approximation to those under the learner policy. As the policies separate, the value of the same action can change and learner trajectories can visit histories poorly represented in the behavior data. The resulting error depends on how far the policies move apart and how much their different choices change the eventual reward. Task structure can change the consequences of policy mismatch. With more learner updates against fixed µ, πθ can change both action probabilities and continuation values further before the sampler is refreshed. sections.title: 7 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: Regularized Score Centering removes the reward baseline contribution and adds reverse KL to penalize movement away from the behavior policy. With this control of policy movement, our analysis connects accurate surrogate fitting to reward improvement. Consistent with this motivation, the experiments show benefits when data come from stale policies and in agentic tasks where actions change subsequent states and rewards. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency on 16 Crafter and Craftax, attaining higher training rewards for the same number of sampled responses. It also achieves top final performance across all six agentic tasks. Its gains over the strongest baselines include 14.3% improvement on AppWorld and 9.9 the score on BabyAI. The software engineering results extend these gains to fully asynchronous training, where policy lag varies over time. The theoretical guarantee also allows token log-ratio radius that does not shrink with the response horizon and, for unit weights, accommodates Monte Carlo estimates of the center. Building on these guarantees, useful direction for future work is to study how greater policy staleness affects RSC empirically, including how many optimizer updates are needed to maintain reward improvement as the learner moves further from the policies that generated the data.
